Location: Bidur, Nepal

Disaster: Floods, 2026

Isha Rimal is a 17-year-old volunteer for the Red Cross Society in Bidur, Nepal. This summer, her family was caught up in the floods that crashed through the country after a glacier collapsed – an event made more likely by climate change

From the roof of our home we can see the Himalayan goddesses. That is what the mountains mean to us: they are goddesses. I grew up here in Bidur, Nuwakot, two hours from Kathmandu. It is a beautiful place with a perfect climate. Or so I used to think, before the Bhotekoshi flood waters from the glacier collapse tore down the Trishuli River, destroyed many homes and killed some of my friends.

View image in fullscreen Isha has volunteered with the Red Cross Society since the disaster.

It changed my life. Until then I had planned to study in the US and become a neuroscientist. But now I want to stay here, train as a medical doctor and help my people.

I thought it was an earthquake at first. The house was shaking. My bed was shaking.

I was alone at home. My younger brother and sister were at school, but I was sleeping in because I’d just graduated. At about 9am I got a call from my mum. She told me to come as fast as I could to the college where she worked. She didn’t say why, but she sounded worried. So I got out of bed, locked the house and left as fast as I could. I only had 10% power on my phone.

View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the flood. Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

It is a 10-minute walk from my home to the college. My mum had told me to hurry, so I ran. Everyone was in a hurry and running. Many were going down towards the river – the opposite direction from me. I remember a strange smell.

I didn’t talk to anyone, so I didn’t know what was happening. All that was going through my head was trying to guess why mum had called me. She had never done that before, not while she was at work.

I never imagined the threat could come from the river. That’s also 10 minutes’ walk from my home. My friends and I used to go there as children. People would bathe there. We live among rivers. They had never been something to be scared of.

When I reached the college, I found my mum. She had been informed about the flood. We never imagined it could be so big. Everybody was chattering; there were rumours that all the buildings had collapsed. Mum started crying. She said my brother and sister’s school had been affected, and she hadn’t been able to reach them.

It is difficult for me to remember all my frightened feelings at that time. We didn’t know if we were safe. We learned the bridge had been washed away, so there was no way to go to the other side. There were rumours of more floods. And my brother and sister were missing.

We had no way of knowing where they had gone. Police had turned up at their school in Bidur and told the students to flee. Teachers packed as many as they could in the school bus, but there was only one bus and hundreds of students. The others were just told to run as fast as they could. We asked a relative to look for them on a motorbike. He found my sister. But my brother took more time. He had hitched a lift with some foreigners and reached very high ground. We were crying with worry, and it turned out he had been eating ice-cream!

View image in fullscreen A debris-strewn residential street after the devastating flash floods in Devighat, Nuwakot. Photograph: Sunil Pradhan/Anadolu/Getty Images

When the river calmed, we went home. But everything was chaotic. The flood had knocked out two hydropower plants. The phone signals in many areas were down, and there was no electricity. The fans and air conditioning didn’t work, so it was too hot to sleep at night. There was also so much noise from the rescue helicopters.

It has been traumatic. Many died. One of my childhood friends was killed. Others lost their homes. After a while, the bodies of dead people and animals started to smell. Many people are psychologically affected by what happened, by seeing the collapsed homes. My brother and sister were so scared that we sent them to Kathmandu for four days.

Two days later, we had another flood. I don’t think anyone reported it. From then on, there were constant rumours about other floods. And fake alerts, even at 2am. These made people evacuate, and some homes were robbed.

View image in fullscreen Houses partly submerged in muddy water along the riverside at Trishuli Bazar in Nuwakot. Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty Images

I didn’t dare visit the disaster area for many weeks. When I finally got the courage, I was shocked to see that places in Devighat I used to visit were gone. A temple where I had worshipped, gardens where our family had spent happy times together, markets where we used to shop, all gone. All those memories, gone.

I volunteered for the Red Cross. At first I worked for 30 days in the pharmacy of the emergency clinic. With the local bridge broken, many community members were left stranded and unable to reach Trishuli hospital for urgent care. As a volunteer, I’ve been on the ground assisting our pharmacists with medical inventory, listing treatments and dispensing free medicine directly to those in need.

Seeing people leave our clinic relieved, happy and deeply grateful to the Red Cross for providing what they needed most during this disaster has been the most rewarding experience.

After that, I trained with the sanitation team and learned how to advise people to wash their hands and use water purification tablets. This was important, because many water sources were contaminated.

In some areas the need is still very great. There were many NGOs here immediately after the flood, but most of them have gone. I guess there was no way for them to leave enough for everyone for a lifetime. But many didn’t even provide for five months.

I will continue volunteering until the end of December, then I will go to Kathmandu to study for my entrance exam for medical school.

My thinking has changed. I used to think that life was sorted, and now I have seen how quickly people can be affected. I used to want to be a neuroscientist and have fun in New York, but after seeing the doctors in the clinic I want to help people like they do. I love that. Now I feel happy to stay here and distribute medical treatment. It makes me feel happy when people thank me for doing that. I realise now that I don’t want to leave my country. I want to be here. I want to be a good doctor.

But we must change things. I still love mountains, but now I think people must be more respectful of mountains. We should not treat the climate as a big joke. We shouldn’t mess with it. The Bhotekoshi flood proved that climate change does not respect borders. While our nation contributes almost nothing to global emissions, our people are left rebuilding their lives inside cracked and damaged walls. I think other countries should take more responsibility, but we cannot be negligent here. This is a sign. We need to take the climate as a serious issue. Everyone around the world should do what they can. I am not asking for donations for Nepal; I am asking that everyone minimise the way they are affecting us. If we continue to ignore the melting Himalayas today, the consequences will flow down to everyone’s doorstep tomorrow.

title: Wild Elephants Cause Fear in Nepal Border Villages - Ratopati
description: Wild Elephants Cause Fear in Nepal Border Villages  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Jhapa. Fear has spread in the villages on the Nepal side after 14 wild elephants took shelter in the no-man's land area of Mechinagar Municipality-7 today all day. The no-man's land area where the elephants took shelter has bushes of sissoo and teak saplings growing in the Indian territory to the east. On the Nepal side, there are dense human settlements like Satighatta, Mechibasti, and Gairigaon.

Eyewitness GR Dhital said that a herd of elephants, including small calves, was seen in the bushes near the no-man's land since this morning. He said, "Those elephants have been staying there all day. We are afraid they might enter the village at any time."

To prevent the elephants from entering the settlements on the Nepal side, the Armed Police Force No. 2 Battalion, various BOPs, and security personnel deployed from the Division Forest Office Jhapa have increased security deployment at the border, said Ram Bhagat Yadav, acting chief of the Division Forest Office Jhapa.

Although the elephants coming from India have been stopped at the border, the local residents are afraid that the herd might enter the village at night. The members of 18 families in the Indian settlement east of the bushes where the elephants took shelter have left their homes since morning. Some of the residents of the Indian settlement who left their homes to save their lives are taking shelter in houses on the Nepal side, while some have gone to India via a roundabout route in Nepal.

The District Administration Office Jhapa had stated that security personnel have been deployed in the border area since Wednesday to stop the herd of elephants trying to enter Nepal from Prasad Gauda of Mechinagar-4.

The herd of elephants, which could not enter Nepal from the Bahunḍaṅgā border area of Mechinagar-4, changed its route and has been relocated to Mechinagar-7 from under the Mechi bridge about five kilometers south.

Chief District Officer Shravan Kumar Pokharel informed that security has been heightened on the Indian side to send the elephants back to India after elephants entered Nepal from Indian territory, destroying local residents' houses and eating ripe paddy.

To completely prevent the entry of elephants and to avoid potential damage, the Armed Police Force, Nepal Police, forest rangers from the Division Forest Office, Rapid Response Team, various organizations, and local farmers have been actively involved.

title: Nepal still has few large employers after 35 years of liberalisation - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal still has few large employers after 35 years of liberalisation  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
More than three and a half decades after Nepal embraced economic liberalisation, the country has failed to develop enough large employers to absorb its growing workforce, forcing around 2,000 young people to seek jobs abroad every day.

Economic reforms were introduced to encourage private investment, production, and trade. But political instability, internal conflict, inadequate infrastructure, and weak governance have prevented the country from creating enough jobs.

Prakash Kumar Shrestha, a former vice-chairman of the National Planning Commission, said the deteriorating investment climate and the government’s inability to increase capital expenditure in recent years had directly affected job creation.

“Investment in the service sector has expanded somewhat in recent years, but it generates relatively fewer jobs,” he said. “Significant employment opportunities come when investment expands in industrial and manufacturing sectors. Those sectors remain weak in Nepal.”

Nepal has had 32 governments in the 35 years since multi-party democracy was restored in 1990. Around 500,000 young people enter the labour market every year, yet the number of business groups directly employing more than 10,000 people remains small.

Golchha Organisation, Chaudhary Group, IME Group, Vishal Group, Shankar Group, Golyan Group, Triveni Group, and Bhatbhateni Supermarket are among the country’s largest private-sector employers. Their investments span industry, trade, financial services, energy, manufacturing, agriculture, tourism, and retail. Some employ more than 20,000 people directly.

Although these business groups have created employment, their combined contribution is not enough to absorb the pressure on the wider labour market. While new workers continue to enter the workforce, established businesses are struggling to expand investment and production capacity. Businessmen and entrepreneurs say Nepal has failed to attract new industrial enterprises capable of employing thousands of people over the past decade. Even existing factories are not operating at full capacity.

According to Shrestha, private-sector credit growth of around five to six percent in recent years, coupled with weak government capital expenditure, has further restricted opportunities for new jobs.

The expansion of the service sector has also been concentrated largely in trade, hospitality, and traditional financial services. Investment in higher-value sectors such as information technology, knowledge-based services, innovation, artificial intelligence, data centres, and digital technologies remains below expectations.

Bhatbhateni Supermarket, a major retail sector employer, currently employs more than 10,000 people. Post Photo

Despite these constraints, some major private-sector employers continue to provide jobs to thousands of people within the country.

Chandra Prasad Dhakal, chairman of IME Group and a former president of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, said around 20,000 people were currently employed directly across the group’s businesses. More than 1,000 additional jobs are expected once the group’s projects under construction become operational.

“More than 81 percent of total employment in the country comes from the private sector. Since the private sector bears the main responsibility for creating jobs, the government must create an environment conducive to investment expansion,” Dhakal said. “Although good policies and commitments to reform are announced, the failure to implement them has undermined private sector confidence.”

Golchha Organisation also says it employs more than 10,000 people directly. One of Nepal’s oldest business groups, its investments began with jute mills and have since expanded into steel, food products, sugar, electrical goods, automobiles, financial services and technology.

Ramlal Golchha was one of the promoters of Biratnagar Jute Mills, Nepal’s first industrial enterprise. The family’s fourth generation is now involved in the business.

“More than 10,000 people are directly employed across our group,” said Abhimanyu Golchha, a director of Golchha Group. “If the investment climate improves and businesses can expand, we can create even more jobs.”

Chaudhary Group says it directly employs around 15,000 people in Nepal. Its investments cover food and beverages, hotels, financial services, energy, education, and manufacturing. The group is also pursuing several projects, including a chemical fertiliser plant, which are expected to generate additional employment once operational, said its general manager, Madhusudan Poudel.

Triveni Group employs more than 15,000 people, according to director Aditya Sanghai. The group aims to create another 300 to 500 jobs over the next three years. Projects including cable cars and hydropower plants are under construction and are expected to add to its workforce once completed.

Shankar Group also says it provides direct employment to around 15,000 people through more than 100 businesses and industrial enterprises. Its investments span steel, cement, automobiles, financial services, agriculture, and hydropower.

Bhatbhateni Supermarket is a major retail sector employer. Chief Executive Officer Panu Poudel said the company currently employs more than 10,000 people. It is working to reopen stores damaged during last year’s Gen Z protests and open four new outlets. The company expects to generate another 2,000 to 2,500 jobs over the next year and a half.

Golyan Group also reports more than 10,000 direct employees. Its investments span agriculture, manufacturing, renewable energy, and hospitality. Chairman Akshay Golyan said the group plans to create additional jobs through Reliance Spinning Mills and its energy and hotel businesses.

These examples show the potential of private-sector expansion to create large numbers of jobs within Nepal. But the failure to foster an environment that encourages fresh investment and industrial growth continues to limit that potential.

Foreign employment figures underline the scale of the challenge. In the fiscal year 2024-25, Nepal issued more than 839,000 labour permits for overseas employment. The figure includes both new and renewed permits, and reflects the country’s reliance on foreign labour markets and the shortage of job opportunities at home.

Remittances from migrant workers contribute to foreign exchange reserves, boost consumption, and help reduce poverty. But the continued departure of skilled and semi-skilled workers also increases the risk of labour shortage for domestic industries. Over time, this could affect Nepal’s production capacity, human capital, and competitiveness.

Shrestha said the government needs to increase capital expenditure, encourage private investment, and ensure markets for domestically produced goods. Manufacturing cannot expand without export promotion, infrastructure development and policy stability, he said.

Economic liberalisation in Nepal was intended to make the private sector the driving force of the economy. Yet, 35 years later, the country has still failed to develop enough large employers. Policy uncertainty, administrative hurdles, inadequate infrastructure, high industrial production costs, and limited market access continue to discourage business expansion.

title: Holiday Travel in Nepal Marked by Overpriced Fares and Reckless Driving - Ratopati
description: Holiday Travel in Nepal Marked by Overpriced Fares and Reckless Driving  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. As the festivals approach, the roads become busy. During the festivals, those leaving their workplaces increase. Especially those leaving Kathmandu are more numerous.

But looking at the condition of Nepal's roads, traveling is like winning a war, and on top of that, there is the compulsion to pay double the fare. There is mistreatment by drivers and conductors, and on the way. There is not enough cleanliness in the hotels where food is eaten, nor is it available at a fair price. But all this has become the destiny of ordinary Nepalis.

As soon as the festival begins, a crowd of people returning to their villages from Kathmandu starts. Transportation entrepreneurs and middlemen consider this crowd an opportunity to make money. Artificial scarcity is created at ticket counters, and black marketing begins.

Vehicles leaving Kathmandu are charging up to double the fare. The situation is the same when people return to their workplaces in Kathmandu after the major festivals like Dashain, Tihar, and Chhath. The common people fall into this double blow. This problem has not been solved or stopped for years.

On Thursday morning, an EV vehicle with Madhesh Province 03-001 Ja 0880, which left Tikaathali in Lalitpur, met with an accident in Bhimfedi-6. The vehicle, which was going towards Sarlahi around 5:45 am, had fallen about 700 meters down the road.

000

Ramchandra Shivakoti travels to and from Kathmandu-Hetauda every month for business. The regular Sumo fare from Hetauda to Kathmandu is 750 rupees. If you travel by electric vehicle (EV), the fare is even cheaper. Ramchandra says, 'In normal times, one can travel at the fixed fare. But, taking advantage of the festival, vehicles are charging one thousand rupees per person as a matter of course.' He claims that the fare from Kathmandu to Hetauda reached up to 1500 during Dashain.

He also recounted arguing at the counter about the fare. He cited government regulations, but received a rude response from the counter staff. 'If you want to go, go, otherwise leave the road, hundreds of passengers are in line to pay this much money,' Shivakoti complains, 'Nothing could be done in the face of haste and compulsion.'

The problems faced by passengers during festivals are not limited to financial exploitation. After paying a high fare, the passengers' faint hope of at least a safe and peaceful journey is dashed once they reach the road. Festival travelers have to endure extreme negligence by vehicle drivers, uncivil behavior, and races that endanger their lives. Especially in short and medium-distance vehicles, a dangerous trend is prevalent – the greed for another trip. In the greed to reach the destination quickly and return, and to carry another group of passengers and earn a lot of money, drivers are turning the roads into death traps.

Sushma Magar, a passenger met at Balkhu, was returning from Kathmandu to her home in Sarlahi this Tihar. She said that she had to come via Hetauda instead of BP Highway and was forced to pay a high fare. Moreover, she was scared remembering the uncontrolled speed of the microbus driver. 'The driver drives as if he has to overtake any vehicle,' she says, 'without reducing speed at any turn.'

She recounts that even when requested to drive slowly, the driver would not listen and would instead get annoyed.

Overtaking, overspeeding, and complete violation of traffic rules have become commonplace on the highways. Due to such negligence by drivers and the race to make another trip, road accidents increase sharply during the festival season.

Arbitrary Fares in Kathmandu

It is not only the passengers traveling out of Kathmandu who are facing such extreme problems. The condition of ordinary people traveling within the Kathmandu Valley is even more pathetic. Suresh Thing, who lives in Kathmandu, finds it very difficult to reach his office and visit relatives during the festival. The minimum fare set by the government has no meaning during the festival.

'Places where the fare is 20 rupees, they directly ask for 25 or 30 rupees,' Suresh said, recounting many arguments with the conductor about the fare, 'When asked why 25 was taken instead of 20 rupees, they speak disrespectfully. Sometimes they say they don't have change, sometimes they say it's the festival season, it's like this.'

Government is a Spectator

Even though passengers are enduring so much hardship and fraud, the police, administration, and government are nowhere to be seen. Consumer rights activist Sapana Sinjali Magar says, 'Before the festival begins, the government holds meetings with transport entrepreneurs. Although administrative offices and the Department of Transport Management issue notices not to charge more than the fixed fare, not to carry more passengers than the seat capacity, and that strict action will be taken for violations, they are not implemented even a bit in practice.'

Magar says that even though incidents of openly charging high fees are happening in various places in Kathmandu, the police are not seen taking action.

We are taking action as soon as we know: Traffic Police

Naresh Raj Subedi, Information Officer and Superintendent of Police (SP) at the Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office, says that the responsibility for arbitrary fare collection lies jointly with the Transport Management Office and the Traffic Police. Subedi says, 'We have arranged special checks in Hetauda, Kathmandu, Balkhu area, and other major junctions and entry points of transportation. However, complaints of lack of monitoring or secretly charging higher fares are still coming from some places, and we are serious about these issues.'

SP Subedi adds that they are committed to taking immediate action if any passenger has to pay more than the fixed rate or is cheated, 'We have taken action as per the information received or complaints made. But if any transport entrepreneur is found to have charged more than the fixed rate or cheated passengers, and if the official number or evidence is provided, we will take legal action immediately.'

He emphasized that both the public and transport workers must follow the rules to prevent the practice of forcing passengers and charging higher fares by taking advantage of the festival season, going against the law. Charging more than the rate set by the government by public transport vehicles is completely against the law.

An Indian tourist died in the accident involving aircraft operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty; three others, including both pilots, were injured in the crash.

At a Glance Nepal total: 429 tigers in 2026.

429 tigers in 2026. Banke: 51, up from 25 in 2022.

51, up from 25 in 2022. Chitwan area: 145, the highest count.

145, the highest count. Bardiya: 112, down from 125.

112, down from 125. India’s Manas: 58 in 2022, up from 11.

Park by Park

Parsa National Park recorded the largest rise, to 71 tigers from 41, and Shuklaphanta National Park went to 50 from 36, the Kathmandu Post reported. Chitwan National Park and its surrounding areas recorded 145 tigers, up from 128. Bardiya National Park, with 112, was the only park where numbers fell, from 125 in 2022.

The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation released the results on July 29, Global Tiger Day, and the count was done with camera traps between December 31 and April 23, the Kathmandu Post said.

The Banke Story

Banke had an estimated four tigers in 2013, Travel PR News reported. The park lies in Lumbini Province within the Terai Arc Landscape, a cross border area where tigers move through forests, buffer zones and wildlife corridors. Earlier transfers of tigers from Chitwan helped establish populations in Banke and Shuklaphanta, a conservation official told Spotlight Nepal, according to the report.

Across the Border in India

Manas, in Assam, rose from 11 tigers in 2014 to 58 in 2022, and Pettitts Travel projects 104 by 2030, the fastest percentage rise among the Indian reserves it ranked, Travel PR News reported. UNESCO removed Manas Wildlife Sanctuary from its list of World Heritage in Danger in 2011 after years of recovery work. India’s national estimate stood at 3,682 tigers in 2022, more than double the 1,411 counted in 2006.

Planning a tiger trip in India instead? Read our story on Ranthambore’s park zones reopening.

A Word of Caution

The 2030 figures are forecasts, and the study itself notes that tiger density alone cannot predict sightings, Travel PR News reported. The study drew on census estimates from 53 Indian reserves and five Nepalese parks. A growing population in a park does not guarantee you will see a tiger on any given drive, so plan for several game drives rather than one.

Choosing a Park

Chitwan has the most tigers and the most developed lodges and access, which makes it the simplest first choice. Bardiya, with 112 tigers, offers a more remote experience. Banke is newer to safari travel and its recovery is recent, so check with an operator about lodges, guides and access before planning around it.

Planning Tips

Nepal’s Terai parks are usually visited in the cooler, drier months, and many operators favor the spring, when grass is cut back and visibility improves. Neither source covered seasons or permits, so confirm park entry rules, fees and guide requirements with your operator. Bring binoculars and neutral clothing, and expect early morning starts.

Who It Suits

Wildlife travelers who want a strong chance of tigers in Nepal should start with Chitwan or Bardiya, while repeat visitors looking for a quieter park may want to explore Banke. Travelers who want guaranteed sightings will be disappointed, since no wild park can promise them.

The Numbers

Nepal’s tiger count rose 74 from 2022 to 2026, about 21 percent. Banke more than doubled, while Lumbini Province, home to Banke and Bardiya, held 163 tigers combined in 2026, Travel PR News reported.

The Decision for Your Trip

If you want the best odds of seeing a tiger in Nepal, book several game drives in Chitwan or Bardiya. If you want to see a recovery story up close and can accept fewer facilities, ask an operator about Banke, and treat the 2030 projections as hopes rather than promises.
